newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shrugs off Deng's death as handover looms.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shrugs off Deng's death as handover looms.

text.p: Busy Hong Kong shrugged off news of Deng Xiaoping's death on Thursday and went about its business as people and the stock market discounted fears of instability just 131 days before the territory reverts to China.
"I think it won't make any big difference to the financial or political point of view," said office worker Mimi Chow.

Some political analysts had predicted Deng's death would create uncertainty in Hong Kong and threaten stability during its delicate transition to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years as a British colony.

British flags flew at half-mast and newspapers splashed "Deng Dead" across their front pages. The South China Morning Post printed an eight-page midday edition on Deng, the newspaper's first extra since Hong Kong's Legislative Council elections in September 1995.
But the news cast few ripples across Hong Kong's daily bustle.
"I think people are complacent," said shop manager Jean Ramsay. Few customers had been talking about Deng, she said.
Shop assistant Pam Yau, who was born in Hong Kong but brought up in Britain, had no interest in Deng or his death.
"Who's he?" the 23-year-old said.
Deng is credited with transforming China from an improverished Stalinist state into an emerging economic powerhouse, and spurring the economy of neighbouring Hong Kong along the way.
But he is also remembered in Hong Kong for the bloody crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989, which led a million protestors to take to the streets of the territory.

Hong Kong stocks slumped early on the news but then shot higher throughout the day, shaking off what brokers said was uncertainty over the state of Deng's health that had plagued the market over the past few sessions. The blue-chip Hang Seng Index ended 2.33 percent higher at 13,411.33.
Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities, said "the last detectable uncertainty in China has been removed with the death of Deng Xiaoping".
But the Post warned of a possible power struggle in Beijing.
"Although Deng's death is unlikely to result in a major immediate policy shift over Hong Kong, changes in the corridors of power in Beijing will spill over into the territory," the newspaper said.
Political analysts said it would take some time to see how Chinese President Jiang Zemin would consolidate his power.

"I don't think it's going to be plain sailing for Jiang Zemin," said political commentator Philip Bowring. "You're going to see, in the first instance at any rate, a collective style of leadership, at least until Jiang is sufficiently his own man that he can dispose of those around him."

Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten paid his respects to Deng at the Xinhua news agency, Beijing's de facto mission in Hong Kong, and was followed inside by Tung Chee-hwa, who takes the helm of the territory on July 1.

Tung, flanked by members of his inner cabinet, bowed three times to a large black and white photograph of Deng, who died late on Wednesday at the age of 92 of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
Martin Lee, chairman of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, said he hoped Chinese leaders would take a softer line on Hong Kong in the wake of Deng's death.

"China simply wants to control Hong Kong, which is exactly the opposite of what Deng Xiaoping intended in 1984 -- which is, Hong Kong people will be ruling Hong Kong with a high degree of autonomy. That means a hands-off policy as opposed to the hands-on policy of today," Lee told Hong Kong radio from London.
Ordinary people marked Deng's passing in their own way.
"I couldn't sleep well the whole night. He was a great leader of our nation. He improved China," said Ko Chiu, 80, after practising tai chi, or Chinese shadow boxing.
But Auyeung Pak, 85, paused from his slow jog in a Hong Kong park to shrug off Deng's death.
"It's normal for a man of that old age. I'm not too sad."
